title: My AI game releases today!
author: Embarrassed_Text_347
selftext:
I've been working on **Core Crusher**, a top-down roguelite built around a pretty simple idea: instead of making each level harder by just giving enemies more HP, every sector introduces a different mechanic.

There are 50 handcrafted sectors in total. Some flood the arena with swarms, some reflect your own bullets back at you, some disable weapons, and others completely change how you have to approach the fight.

One place AI ended up being useful during development was the art pipeline. For some enemies, I'd first make my own rough mockup/design for what I wanted, then use generative AI to help turn that concept into artwork I could actually use in-game. I didn't have it just create sprite icons, but rather used it to dynamically create them with godot's basic geometry. I also used it to assist with some of the store assets.

That workflow was especially useful as a solo dev because I could still decide the enemy's shape, purpose, and general look myself without needing to be good enough at digital art to create every finished asset from scratch.

The game releases on Steam today, so I'm interested to see how people respond to it now that it's finally out.

I'd also be curious how other solo devs here handle this. If you're using AI for art, do you start from your own sketches/mockups, generate from scratch, or use it mostly for iteration?

Steam: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/4908610/Core\_Crusher/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4908610/Core_Crusher/)

comments.author: drnktgr
comments.body: I'm sure we're all curious too to see how this release goes. Congrats on the release! And you went for a very attractive price. I'll keep my eyes on this one.

replies.author: Embarrassed_Text_347
replies.body: Thank you! I don't have a huge marketing team or anything really, so any support is super appreciated <3. Just been trying to get it out there myself here and there.

comments.author: emperormarkus
comments.body: This looks very cool. Can I ask how long it took you and what your process was?

replies.author: Embarrassed_Text_347
replies.body:
It took me roughly 6 weeks from start to finish. I was working around 50 hours a week on it, with some breaks here and there. There was a lot of growing pains and the game changed direction quite a bit during the development process.

I have a CS degree and have been building web-based games for the past 3-4 years or so. This was my first attempt with a real game engine. In the past, I attempted to get into it but it was pretty daunting considering I had no experience with GDScript or Godot. I tried a few tutorials and gave up. 

Nowadays, with codex, especially the new models it's more of supervising the agents. I gave it another go, I already have the game-dev background with the web games so I knew how games are supposed to feel, how important ui is, sounds, ux, etc. and so I basically supervised an agent and went feature by feature, building out the entire game. It took a while, and there were many times where I was banging my head against the wall, but overall it did an amazing job putting my ideas into place.

As much as people will continue to hate on generative ai, it's here to stay. It's so impressive what the capabilities are, and it's only going to improve from here. I think it's super exciting, someone with 0 Godot coding experience, building and shipping a steam game from start to finish :).

replies.author: emperormarkus
replies.body: That’s a good investment of time. The output at a glance looks very cool. Let us know how the experience on Steam goes.

replies.author: Embarrassed_Text_347
replies.body: Will do. I've always wanted to ship a game on steam. I doubt this will pay the bills, but I'm glad I'm doing it. 😄

replies.author: UpDown
replies.body: What’s your full set up? Are you using ai in godot? Or making gdscriots in VSCode? Not familiar with your set up but results look good

replies.author: Embarrassed_Text_347
replies.body: Used codex in vscode with access to the full godot project, it was able to write and test there.

replies.author: Flash1987
replies.body: Pretty different story to your AI disclosure...

replies.author: Embarrassed_Text_347
replies.body: I see your point. The way I read steam's AI disclosure is that it's for ai-generated user-facing assets (images and sound, typically). Most of the game is simple geometry from godot's built-in kit. If I was using it for image generation, I would disclose that. It is simply writing the code, rather than creating assets. Even the enemies are drawn in with simple godot shapes. There isn't any "ai-generated artwork" inside of the game at all. I did think putting in some sort of disclosure was necessary though, so I chose to specify the enemies as "ai generated" even though they are really just a few lines of gdscript.

comments.author: trieckaga
comments.body: Mine as well! Today is the day. Gongrats! Good luck with the release!

comments.author: KingVorpal
comments.body: Are you familiar with the concept of paint pallets? I tried to use AI but it was drawing me Picasso pictures I couldn’t animate and just looked weird next to my assets I drew by hand. So I fed it a bunch of my work and told it “don’t draw better than this” and I had to really beat it into submission to make it draw what I wanted. Eventually I wound up using the nicer portraits to make brushes and colors so all my art looks consistent. I’m still making a lot of assets by hand because it draws to good and I needed stuff I could animate and re draw myself over and over again like a cartoon artist does. It’s fun. I still wish I had a real artist to work with at times but at least my art is consistent. I felt like consistently was more important than quality. Also I underestimated the power of making my own sounds and music. A good track can really make or break a setting.
